query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, high-temperature oxidation‐ and corrosion‐resistant ceramic coating (e.g., zirconia-based) to AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA fasteners will improve their resistance to surface-initiated creep and corrosion under extreme temperature fluctuations and long-term mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure as produced by conventional casting, currently exhibiting a good strength–ductility balance but limited resistance to surface degradation under harsh conditions.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin ceramic coating designed for high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance onto the fastener surfaces.
generation.conditions: Service conditions typical of aircraft and spacecraft fasteners, including cyclic temperature fluctuations (up to approximately 700°C), prolonged mechanical loading (to simulate creep), and exposure to corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal, adherent ceramic coating that forms a coherent interface with the alloy surface without altering the underlying lamellar microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The coating acts as a barrier against oxygen, moisture, and corrosive species, while also mitigating surface stress concentrations that can trigger creep deformation. This preserves the bulk mechanical properties by preventing the initiation of surface degradation phenomena.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated fasteners will show improved long-term stability with reduced creep rates and corrosion damage as compared to uncoated ones, thereby extending the operational life of the fasteners without compromising the alloy's inherent strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Uncoated AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA fasteners that, while mechanically robust and ductile in the bulk, are prone to surface degradation (corrosion and creep initiation) under extreme service conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected provided that the ceramic coating remains stable (no cracking or delamination) under the defined thermal and mechanical cycling and the deposition process does not negatively affect the bulk microstructure of the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement in creep and corrosion resistance is uncertain and may be influenced by potential issues such as thermal expansion mismatches between the coating and substrate, which could lead to delamination or crack propagation under cyclic loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of fastener samples: one set with the ultrathin ceramic coating applied, and one set uncoated. Subject both sets to accelerated environmental testing that includes cyclic temperature fluctuations (room temperature to 700°C), constant mechanical loading for creep assessment, and exposure to a corrosive medium. After testing, analyze the samples for surface degradation (using microscopy and weight loss measurements), creep deformation, and retention of mechanical strength.
measurements: Microstructural integrity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) or transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
Residual tensile strength and ductility after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ceramic-coated fasteners do not show a statistically significant improvement in either creep resistance or corrosion resistance (i.e., similar degradation metrics or premature coating failure such as crack propagation or delamination) compared to the uncoated baseline, then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Given the energy-efficient improvement and large safety factors, the attainment of high strength and high ductility in materials is arguably a vital requirement for most engineering applications. Unfortunately, these two properties are generally mutually exclusive, particularly in pure metals and alloys. Eutectic alloys specifically exhibit good liquidity and castability, preventing common casting flaws, like internal shrinkage and compositional segregation, to downgrade mechanical properties. They also possess a regularly arranged lamellar organization that can be viewed as a natural or in situ composite, which enables synergetic reinforcement to improve mechanical properties and sometimes bring unusual electrical, magnetic, and optical behaviors. Eutectic materials have therefore been investigated in diverse application fields, but traditionally, only certain eutectic systems have been of major commercial importance. Recently, eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), first proposed by Lu et al. in 2014, were designed based on the above eutectic-alloy concept. The high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a new alloy with more than four main elements. In recent years, HEAs have attracted attention due to their outstanding performance, including superior mechanical properties, abrasion resistance, and corrosion resistance [,]. Single-phase body-centered-cubic (BCC) and face-centered-cubic (FCC) HEAs have been the subject of much research over the past decade. Several studies have reported that BCC HEAs possess high strength, while FCC HEAs are highly ductile. According to comprehensive research, it is difficult to achieve both high strength and ductility in single-phase HEAs [,,]. To further improve the properties of HEA, Lu et al. [,] proposed the concept of eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) that combined the strength of BCC HEAs and ductility of FCC HEAs. EHEAs have broad application prospects due to their excellent mechanical properties over a wide temperature range [,,]. However, EHEA research mainly focuses on mechanical properties, while there are few studies on the corrosion behavior of EHEAs. reading.lever: Apply an ultrathin, high‐temperature oxidation- and corrosion‐resistant ceramic coating to the EHEA fasteners.
reading.why: Such a surface intervention can directly mitigate corrosion and creep initiation at the surface under extreme conditions without altering the engineered bulk microstructure.
